github-actions-security.text:
Our CI workflow runs on pull requests, also from forks, and uploads an artifact `coverage` with `pr-number.txt` and `report.md`. Review this second workflow for security problems.

```yaml
name: Coverage comment
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [CI]
    types: [completed]
permissions:
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  comment:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage
          run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }}
          github-token: ${{ github.token }}
      - name: Load results
        run: |
          echo "PR_NUMBER=$(cat pr-number.txt)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "REPORT<<EOF" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          cat report.md >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "EOF" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Post comment
        run: gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --body "$REPORT"
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
```
github-actions-security.pass: The answer says that the artifact comes from a run that a fork can control, so its content is untrusted. It reports the write of `report.md` to `GITHUB_ENV` with a fixed delimiter as high or critical, because the content can close the delimiter and set more variables in a job that has a write token. It reports that `pr-number.txt` must be checked as a number before use. The fix does not write artifact content to `GITHUB_ENV`, and passes the report as a file (for example `--body-file`). It does not say that this workflow runs the code of the pull request.

secure-coding.type: safe: fixed command, ORM filter, random tip, fixed URL, escaping template
secure-coding.text:
Review this FastAPI router for security problems.

```python
import random
import subprocess

import httpx
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from jinja2 import Environment, PackageLoader, select_autoescape
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from .auth import get_current_user
from .db import get_session
from .models import Melding
from .settings import settings

router = APIRouter()
templates = Environment(loader=PackageLoader("app"), autoescape=select_autoescape())


@router.get("/versjon")
def versjon() -> dict:
    commit = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
    ).stdout.strip()
    return {"commit": commit}


@router.get("/meldinger")
def meldinger(user=Depends(get_current_user), db: Session = Depends(get_session)) -> list[dict]:
    rader = db.scalars(select(Melding).where(Melding.mottaker_id == user.id)).all()
    tips = random.choice(["Husk fristen.", "Du kan laste opp vedlegg som PDF."])
    return [{"id": m.id, "tekst": m.tekst, "tips": tips} for m in rader]


@router.get("/vaer", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def vaer() -> str:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as client:
        svar = await client.get(settings.vaer_url)
    return templates.get_template("vaer.html").render(data=svar.json())
```
secure-coding.pass: No finding has high or critical severity. The answer does not report the `subprocess.run` call as command injection, `random.choice` as weak randomness, the request to `settings.vaer_url` as SSRF, the ORM query as SQL injection or a missing access check, or the template as XSS. A short answer that finds no real problem is correct. Low notes are acceptable, for example that `/versjon` shows the commit without login.

USER root

universell-utforming.type: plan: first test with blind, eye-control and intellectually disabled participants
universell-utforming.text: Vi er et lite utviklerteam i kommunen og har laget en ny digital søknad om parkeringstillatelse for forflytningshemmede. Før vi lanserer, vil vi teste den med fem personer: to blinde som bruker VoiceOver på iPhone, én med cerebral parese som styrer PC-en med øynene, og to med utviklingshemming. Noen økter blir hjemme hos deltakerne og noen over video. Vi har aldri gjort dette før. Lag en plan for hva vi må gjøre før, under og etter øktene.
universell-utforming.pass: The plan covers these points in words that fit this group. (1) Recruits through the disability organisations, and mixes experienced and less experienced users of assistive technology, not only people who test often. (2) Asks each participant before the session about needs: travel, place, an assistant or companion, how long they can work, and which assistive technology they use. (3) Lets participants use their own equipment, and the team learns how VoiceOver and eye control work before the sessions. (4) Plans more time (up to about double), ranks the tasks so that the most important come first, and plans breaks and when to stop. (5) For the video sessions: a short test call before the session, and the VoiceOver sound must be in the shared audio and in the recording. (6) For the VoiceOver users: agrees how to think aloud while the screen reader talks, can ask for a slower speech rate but notes that this changes their normal pace, and does not read passing an element as failing to find it. (7) Asks for consent to record, says what the recording is for, who sees it and when it is deleted, and treats information about a disability as health data. (8) Covers costs and travel in addition to any gift card. (9) Adapts information, tasks and consent to the participants with intellectual disability, for example with plain language and a person they trust present. (10) Checks that participants understand and get their need solved, not only that they reach the end, and looks at the whole person, not only the disability. (11) Ends each session with a short summary, room for more input, thanks with concrete examples, and a question about later contact. (12) Uses the same tasks and pass criteria as in other tests. (13) Before the sessions, removes the known barriers in the solution, or says how to find them, so that a session does not stop on them. The plan is practical: the team can use it as it is.

universell-utforming.type: review: test plan with gaps and two good parts
universell-utforming.text:
Kan du se over testplanen vår før vi sender ut invitasjonene?

Testplan: brukertest av ny side for å søke om redusert foreldrebetaling i barnehage

- Deltakere: seks personer med synshemming. Vi har bedt et rekrutteringsbyrå om personer fra testpanelet deres som har vært med på mange tester før, så vi slipper å forklare så mye.
- Sted: alle økter går over video. Deltakerne deler skjermen.
- Varighet: 45 minutter per person, satt opp rett etter hverandre fra kl. 9 til 14.
- Oppgaver: åtte oppgaver i fast rekkefølge. Alle skal gjennom alle.
- Instruks: «Tenk høyt mens du jobber, og si hva du ser.»
- Opptak: vi tar opp alle økter.
- Bakgrunn: vi noterer diagnose og synsrest for hver deltaker.
- Godtgjørelse: gavekort på 500 kroner.
- Deltakerne kan ha med en ledsager om de vil, og bruke sin egen PC.
- Bestått: oppgaven er bestått når deltakeren kommer til kvitteringssiden.
universell-utforming.pass: The answer reports these gaps. (1) Only very experienced panel testers: this is a source of error, so mix in less experienced users and recruit through the disability organisations. (2) No question to each participant before the session about needs and how long they can work. (3) 45 minutes back to back is too tight: plan more time, buffers and breaks, and rank the eight tasks so that the most important come first. (4) Screen sharing alone does not carry the screen reader sound: the sound must be shared and recorded, and a test call before the session checks the setup. (5) The instruction 'si hva du ser' does not fit screen reader users: agree how to think aloud while the screen reader talks, and how to follow a fast speech rate. (6) Recording needs consent with the purpose, who sees it and when it is deleted. (7) Diagnosis and remaining sight are health data: collect only what the test needs, and also note experience, assistive technology and expectations, not only the diagnosis. (8) Reaching the receipt page is not enough to pass: the participant must also understand the result and get the need solved. (9) No plan for the end of the session. The answer does not report the companion or the own PC as problems, and does not call video sessions wrong. Covering costs beyond the gift card is a plus, not required.

universell-utforming.text:

Deltaker A (blind, bruker JAWS på PC): Gikk forbi lenken «Bestill time» tre ganger før hen valgte den. Brukte 6 minutter på oppgave 1. Testlederen ba A sette ned talehastigheten i starten så vi kunne følge med. Konklusjon: lenken er vanskelig å finne. Tiltak: flytt den øverst og gjør den større.

Deltaker B (svaksynt, forstørrer skjermen 400 %): Sa at alt gikk fint. Under oppgave 3 kom en feilmelding utenfor det forstørrede området, og B trykket «Send» fire ganger før hen ga opp. B sa etterpå at hen «bare var treg i dag».

Deltaker C (blind, bruker NVDA): Kom til bekreftelsessiden på alle oppgavene. På spørsmål etterpå visste ikke C hvilket klokkeslett timen var bestilt til.

Tidsbruk: A og C brukte i snitt tre ganger så lang tid som deltakerne uten funksjonsnedsettelse. Konklusjon: skjemaet er for tregt for skjermleserbrukere.

A check of the link text and the structure, or a new test, is fine. (2) A's time: the slower speech rate that the moderator asked for makes the time longer, so the time is not a fair measure. (3) The time comparison with participants without disabilities is not a valid basis for 'too slow'. (4) B: a real finding, also when B said that all went well. The error message must show in the enlarged area, or near the field, and be announced (WCAG 1.4.10, 3.3.1 or 4.1.3, or the same in words). The answer does not blame B. (5) C: a real finding. (5) The team learns how the speech device and the switch control work before the sessions, from the participant and from the documentation. (6) Plans more time (up to about double), breaks, the most important tasks first, and when to stop, and does not use the time as a measure for the switch user. (7) Gives the tasks and the information in plain words, also in writing, to the participant with aphasia. (8) Offers an assistant or a session in a room as an alternative to video. (9) Asks for consent to record, and treats the information about the disability and the tools as health data. The plan is practical and in proportion.

universell-utforming.type: transfer: user test plan with remote text-to-speech reader
universell-utforming.text: Hei! Vi er et lite team i kommunen som har laget en ny digital søknad om kommunal bolig. Neste måned skal vi ha brukertester med tre personer: en mann med dysleksi som bruker opplesingsprogram på sin egen PC og vil delta hjemmefra på Teams, en kvinne med sterkt nedsatt syn som forstørrer skjermen mye og bruker høy kontrast, og en kvinne med leddgikt som bare bruker tastatur. De to kvinnene kommer til oss på rådhuset. Vi vil be dem tenke høyt og ta opp skjerm og lyd. Vi har ikke gjort dette før. Kan du lage en plan for øktene og si hva vi må forberede?
universell-utforming.pass: (1) Preparation per participant: before the sessions the team contacts each person and asks about their own setup and needs (reading tool, voice and reading speed; magnification level and contrast mode; preferred keyboard and how long she can work), and does not assume needs from the diagnosis. The man with dyslexia uses his own PC. The two women in the room are offered to bring their own laptop, or the test PC is set up with their settings. The team checks in advance that the service works with these tools at all, and uses a test environment with fictitious data, not real personal data. (2) The reading tool during think-aloud: the plan says that the speech of the tool and the speech of the participant compete. The facilitator does not talk over the tool, accepts silence while it reads, lets the participant decide when the tool reads, and asks for comments after a passage or uses a short retrospective review. What the tool reads, skips or mispronounces is a finding. (3) Remote audio and recording for the man with dyslexia: the facilitator and the recording must get the speech of the tool, his voice and his screen. The plan names the risk (with headphones the microphone does not pick up the tool, and noise suppression can remove it) and a solution (share the screen with computer sound, for example 'include computer sound' in Teams). It tests this in a short technical call before the session and has a fallback, such as a note-taker or a phone line. The meeting link and instructions are short and in a format that his reading tool can read. (4) In the room: the woman with low vision zooms in, so observers need a mirrored or recorded view of the full screen, and the facilitator does not point to 'up and to the right'. Tasks and consent are in large print or in a digital form she can enlarge, or are read aloud. Good light without glare. Accessible arrival: step-free entrance, someone meets them at the reception, short way to the room. The woman with rheumatoid arthritis gets an adjustable chair and table and her preferred or own keyboard, and is never asked to use a mouse. Keyboard problems (focus order, visible focus, keyboard traps) are findings. (5) Time and breaks: longer slots than a standard test, with a buffer for setup (most for the remote session), fewer tasks, planned breaks, and the participant can stop at any time. For the woman with rheumatoid arthritis, pain and fatigue matter: she can choose the time of day, and the session is short or split. (6) Learning the tool: participants use tools that they already know, and nobody must learn a new tool for the test. The team learns the basics of reading software, screen magnification and keyboard navigation and runs a pilot, so that it can tell a problem in the service from a problem with a tool or a setting. The team does not judge the skill of the participant. (7) Consent and health data: information about disability and assistive technology is health data (a special category under GDPR article 9). The team collects only what the test needs, gets explicit informed consent in plain language and in an accessible format, with a separate consent for recording, tells how long data is kept, who sees it and how to withdraw, keeps diagnoses out of the report, stores recordings in approved storage of the municipality, and checks the plan with the data protection officer (personvernombud) before start. It offers compensation. (8) Right advice to the right person: advice about the speech of the tool competing with think-aloud, and about computer sound in a remote session, is for the man with dyslexia only. The plan does not give the women in the room advice about a screen reader, a sign language interpreter or speech output, does not assume that the woman with low vision uses a screen reader, and does not give magnification or ergonomics advice to the man with dyslexia. (9) Conduct and use of results: the facilitator talks directly to the participant, does not help unless asked, and says that the service is tested, not the person. The plan says that three sessions find real problems but do not show WCAG conformance and do not replace an evaluation against WCAG. The plan is practical and in proportion to a small team with three sessions: concrete steps and checks, without padding of general theory, long WCAG lists or advice for needs that no participant has.

universell-utforming.type: review: contrast of the text in a button, written after the rule change (not blind)
universell-utforming.text:
Kan du sjekke denne knappen for universell utforming før vi merger? Siden har hvit bakgrunn.

```css
.btn-primary { background: #4a90d9; color: #ffffff; font-size: 16px; font-weight: 400; padding: 8px 16px; border: none; border-radius: 4px; }
.btn-primary:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1a1a1a; outline-offset: 2px; }
```

```tsx
<button className="btn-primary" type="submit">Send søknad</button>
```
universell-utforming.pass: (1) Reports that the white button text on #4a90d9 has a contrast of about 3.3:1, and that this breaks 1.4.3, because 16px normal-weight text needs 4.5:1, also inside a button. (2) Gives a minimal fix, such as a darker background colour that reaches at least 4.5:1, and keeps the rest of the button. (3) Does not report the edge of the button or the focus outline as a 1.4.11 barrier (the button against the white page is above 3:1, and the dark 3px outline is clearly visible). (4) Does not report false findings for the native button with a visible text name. (5) Short, without content that the user did not ask for.

universell-utforming.type: review: non-text contrast of state and icon, light text button exempt
universell-utforming.pass: (1) Reports the checkbox (.valg) as a 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast failure: the checked state is shown only by the light inner fill #b9cde5, which has about 1.6:1 against the white inset ring (#ffffff) next to it, so the state indicator is below 3:1. Minimal fix: give the checked indicator at least 3:1 against the colours next to it, for example background #1f4e85 (about 8.4:1) in .valg:checked, or add a check mark with at least 3:1. A mention of 1.4.1 for the same checkbox is acceptable, but not as a separate extra barrier. (2) Reports the close button (.lukk) as a 1.4.11 failure: the X icon is the only visual identification of the control, and #9e9e9e has about 2.7:1 against the white background. Minimal fix: a darker icon colour, for example #707070 (about 4.9:1) or darker. The accessible name (aria-label with aria-hidden on the SVG) is correct and is not a finding. (3) No finding for the secondary button "Avbryt". Its fill #e6edf5 has only about 1.2:1 against the page, but 1.4.11 does not require a visible boundary or fill for a button that its text identifies, and the text #1f4e85 has about 7.2:1 against the fill (and about 8.4:1 against the page), so 1.4.3 passes. A 1.4.11 finding, or a statement that the button needs a border or a darker fill, fails this item. (4) No finding about the focus indicator. The CSS removes no outline, so all controls keep the browser default focus style (also the checkbox with appearance: none). 1.4.11 exempts an indicator that the user agent determines and the author does not change, and 2.4.7 is met. (5) No other false findings. Text #222222 on #ffffff (about 15.9:1), the primary button (#ffffff on #1f4e85, about 8.4:1), the unchecked checkbox border (#5c5c5c, about 6.7:1 against white), the label that wraps the checkbox, the heading and the button names all pass. A barrier reported for any of these, or for the div container, the heading level, or two buttons that both close the panel, fails this item. (6) The answer is short: it gives the two barriers with element, criterion, measured ratio and fix, and adds no full audit report, rewritten component, test plan or other content the user did not ask for. Ratios within about 0.1 of the values above are acceptable.
